"Dhālan" is left as written because the plant cannot be identified with confidence. The "measures" obtained in the Supreme Tārā rite translate tshal, an unclear unit. The names of the Tārā forms are translated from their Tibetan, since their Sanskrit forms cannot be fixed with confidence; Pendent Tārā renders sgrol ma 'phyang ba.  "Bāla and kāla eight hundred times each" interprets an unclear phrase (bā la dang so so la ka la). Several results are terse and their sense uncertain: "one drives away vultures" (bya rgod sel ba); "one sports by magical display with the king's chief queen"; "it takes effect on whoever one sees first"; and "in all one's accomplishments one obtains thousands gathered together". "Essences and rejuvenating elixirs" reads the written bcu as bcud.  Several lines of this verse are terse and their sense is uncertain. "Abiding in the kīla" renders phur bu, which could also mean the planet Jupiter (that is, at a Jupiter time). "Rohana birds" renders bya ro ha na, which may be a corrupt or unclear bird name. "Touches them" follows the evident reading reg pa for rig pa ("awareness"), which does not fit the context. In the list of omens, "a cow giving," "hundred-petaled one" (perhaps a lotus or a peacock), "eared one" and "arampa" could not be identified with confidence and are rendered literally.  "One strays from the command of the guru and from the commitment" reads the verb as 'das pa ("transgress"); the text has bzlas pa ("recite"), which makes no sense here. Several verse lines on ritual woods and substances are terse: "pajāka," "vānatra" (written in Sanskrit in the Tibetan) and "with a delay" (bshol ldan) are uncertain, and "this observance" renders an unclear word (mug) taken to refer to the poṣadha vow. The prose passage is the formula for taking the eightfold poṣadha vow.  "Food that is utterly without a fixed abode" renders rab tu mi gnas pa'i bza' ba literally; the intended sense (perhaps food that comes from everywhere, or that never runs out) is unclear. The names of the individual vidyās are translated from the Tibetan, since their Sanskrit forms are not given.  "The king's chaplain" renders mdun na 'don, the standard Tibetan equivalent of purohita, the royal priest and counselor. The names of the individual vidyās are translated from the Tibetan, since their Sanskrit forms are not given.  "One becomes long-lived" takes tsher 'gyur as tshe ring du 'gyur in sense; the phrasing is compressed. The names of the individual vidyās are translated from the Tibetan, since their Sanskrit forms are not given.  The seventh vidyā in this piece is given no name in the Tibetan; only its benefit is stated. In the fourth, "all who roam about" renders རྒྱུ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད, whose precise sense here (wandering beings, or perhaps spies or messengers) is uncertain. The name rendered "Dharma Without Flow" (འབབ་པ་མེད་པ) may reflect a Tibetan understanding of araṇa in the mantra; the literal sense is kept. "The farthest limits" renders མཐའ, which could also mean borderlands or the ends of the earth. "Stationary and moving" poisons are the standard Indian classes sthāvara (plant and mineral) and jaṅgama (animal) poisons.  In the first vidyā, གྲོང་སྟོང་སྡོམ་པ is rendered "a domain of a thousand villages," taking སྡོམ་པ in its sense of a gathered total; the exact sense is uncertain. In the seventh, the subject of "bestow divine medicines" is not stated; it is taken to be the gandharvas just brought under control.  "Hooded serpents" renders གདེངས་ཅན, a standard epithet of nāgas and snakes. "Divine destinies" renders ལྷའི་འགྲོ་བ, the realms of rebirth among the gods.  The heading "vidyā of perfume" reads དྲའི་རིག་པ in the Tibetan; དྲ makes no sense here, and the mantra's gandha points to དྲི, "scent," which is translated. The sentence on "flowers and the rest" is terse; it is taken to mean that the result of offering flowers and so on with this mantra of Dharma Tārā is power over beings. "Bestows lands upon the teachings" renders བསྟན་པ་རྣམས་ལ་ ... ཡུལ་སྦྱིན་པ literally; the intended recipients are uncertain.  The names of the Tārā forms are given in English according to the Tibetan, which renders the key word of each mantra (for example, Tibetan "endowed with the moon" for Sanskrit candramatī). Two forms are distinguished in Tibetan by the honorific "all-seeing" (kun tu gzigs) and the ordinary "all-viewing" (kun du lta ba); the English keeps them apart as "All-Seeing Gaze" and "All-Surveying Vision."  Noble Tārā Endowed with Supreme Wisdom renders Tibetan "endowed with the wisdom of the other (gzhan pa'i shes rab)", which reflects Sanskrit para, "beyond, supreme," in the mantra. Noble Tārā Endowed with the Far-Reaching uses the Tibetan for "gone far" (Skt. dūraṃgamā), the name of the seventh bodhisattva ground. Noble Tārā Endowed with Brahmā renders Tibetan tshangs, the standard rendering of Brahmā or brahma, "pure."  Noble Tārā Spotless Light renders Tibetan "light without eye-salve" (mig sman med pa'i 'od), a literal rendering of Sanskrit nirañjana, "free of collyrium," that is, stainless, as in the mantra. Noble Tārā Power of Moral Discipline is the name the Tibetan gives, although its mantra (bhāse bhāsavatī) speaks of radiance.  In the second name the Tibetan reads yam gyi 'od, which gives no sense; it is evidently a slip for lam gyi 'od, "light of the path," matching mārgaprabhe in its mantra, and is translated so. Noble Tārā Tārā of the Middle Way renders dbu ma'i sgrol ma, matching madhye in the mantra; it could also be understood simply as "Tārā of the Middle."  In the name of the ninth form the Tibetan reads bzar bo, which is not a word; it is evidently a slip for bzang po, "excellent," matching bhadre in the mantra, and the name is rendered as before, Noble Tārā Endowed with Excellence. Noble Tārā Mistress of Generosity renders "lord of giving" (sbyin pa'i bdag po), matching dānapati in the mantra. Noble Tārā Endowed with Lunar Gentleness renders "endowed with moon-ness," a rendering of Sanskrit saumya, "gentle, moonlike."  In the three names rendered "Ordinance of the Buddha, of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha," the Tibetan brtag pa renders Sanskrit kalpa, as the accompanying mantras show (buddhakalpa, dharmakalpa, saṃghakalpa); "ordinance" or "rite" is intended rather than "examination." The epithet rendered "Mistress of Clear Light" corresponds in the mantra to abhisvara, recalling the Ābhāsvara (Clear Light) gods.  "Palāśa wood" renders "brahmā sticks" (tshangs pa'i yam shing), palāśa being known as the brahmā tree. "Aparājitā flowers" renders "flowers that others cannot overcome." The sentence rendered "If one wishes to proceed other than with a painted cloth" could also be read "If one wants another painted cloth." The "digestive pill" (zhu mkhan gyi ril bu) is uncertain. "Milk of a cow of matching lineage" (rgyud mtshungs pa'i 'o ma) and "an equal measure" (gzhan gyi tshad) are uncertain. The text has brgyan for brgyad ("eight") in "eight thousand fire offerings" with aparājitā flowers, and shib, read here as shi ba ("one who has died"). "One struck down by violence" (drag shul la nyams pa) and "lumps of the breast" (nu ma'i phur pa, here not a ritual dagger) are tentative.  Several readings are uncertain: gzhil in the first sentence is taken as gzhi ("ground"); the clause rendered "when one has resolved to paralyze it" is obscure; "siddhārtha wood" (don grub kyi shing) may refer to white mustard. "Realgar bought at a hero's price" renders dpa' bo'i rin gyis nyos pa, apparently meaning bought at whatever price is asked. In the realgar rite, 'gro ba ("goes") is read as dro ba ("becomes warm"), in line with the parallel signs of warmth, smoke and blazing later in the passage. "Superior eye ointment" renders mig sman bla, which is not here the Medicine Buddha. The identities of several substances (bela, khaṇḍaka, "coiling joy plant," rgya spos, "yakṣa's bowl," pucirajata, indra), of the "oppressor spirits" (gnon po), and of "arka sesame oil" are uncertain. The "king tree" and "king of trees" may be the rājavṛkṣa.  Where bcom ldan 'das appears in this Tārā rite (and with bcom ldan 'das ma), it is rendered "the Blessed Lady," since Tārā is clearly the one being worshiped. The clause "it seizes them with binding" (ma nu la 'ching ba 'dzin par byed do) is obscure. "Strike at the three junctures" (thun mtshams gsum du bsnun pa) is literal and its ritual sense unclear. lta mo is read as lha mo ("goddess"). "At first light" renders sngon gyi mtha' ma, which is uncertain. "In full bloom" renders kha rnam par rgyal ba, apparently for kha rnam par rgyas pa. Several plant names (rgya spos, āśibilva, the "thorny plant," "stamen flowers") are uncertain.  "At the battlefield" renders g.yul du, which is unexpected here and may be a slip. "Abstaining from cooked food and salt" reads me dang lan tshwa zos pas ("having eaten fire and salt") as a fasting restriction; the text as written is unclear. The phrase rendered "within a month one will come to be looked upon" (zla ba'i nang du blta bar bya bar 'gyur) is obscure. "Countless times" renders rig pa dpag tu med pa, which might instead name a particular "immeasurable" knowledge mantra. As in the preceding rites, bcom ldan 'das is rendered "the Blessed Lady" where Tārā is meant.  "Through the grace of noble Avalokiteśvara, things will turn out otherwise" renders gzhan du 'gyur ro literally; its sense here (perhaps a change of fortune) is unclear. "Not blackened at its base" (rtsa ba nag po med pa) is a tentative reading. Brahmadāri and jitendraya are given as transliterated in the Tibetan; the plants are not identified with confidence. "Without the preliminary practice" renders bsgrub par bya bzhin pa ma yin pa / sgrub bzhin pa ma yin pa, probably Sanskrit asādhita. "Eye ointment for the ears" (rna ba'i mig sman) is literal and puzzling. The sentence in which the Sauvīra collyrium "becomes a kumbhāṇḍa" (grul bum) follows the house rendering, though kuṣmāṇḍa may here denote a gourd shape; the passage on breaking and disintegration is obscure. The phrase ending "aspiring even to the very summit of all vidyādharas" is uncertain in construction.  "Vases made of cloth" (ras las byung ba) is literal and odd; a scribal slip for an earthenware vessel is possible. The vase name Haring (ha rings) and the foods vakra (wa kra) and hwak (hwags) could not be identified and are kept as they are written. "Concealment from Indra, lord of the gods" (lha'i dbang po sbas pa) is a tentative reading. "Eat only when tormented by suffering" is literal; it probably means eating only when compelled by hunger.  "Except for what has been set aside out of desire" ('dod pas nye bar bzhag pa ma gtogs) is a literal rendering of an obscure phrase, as is "dry cow dung will be cooked into hwak". The Vast Mountain and the Universal Mountain (yangs pa'i ri bo, kun tu ri bo) are titles of ritual manuals that could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally. In the verses, several of the descriptive phrases (entirely white, white parasol, radiating, mass of splendor, invincible, Victor's uṣṇīṣa) closely match the names of the uṣṇīṣa kings Sitātapatra, Vikiraṇa, Tejorāśi, Aparājita and Jayoṣṇīṣa, and may be meant as their names. The line "what is set in its center is not the center" is literal and obscure.  The verses on the mudrā emblems are terse and several lines are uncertain, especially "the one facing forward" (sngon phyogs), "the utpala is also the moon's", the "garland-purifier" line, and the vedī lines (bi dī, probably Skt. vedī or vedikā, a railing or border). "The Victorious One" and "the Fully Victorious One" (rgyal ba, rnam par rgyal) are probably the goddesses Jayā and Vijayā. The prose description of the vajra-family samaya mudrā is obscure, and the closing phrase calling it a "mantra" is translated as written. The "great comforter" (dbugs 'byin chen po) is taken as an epithet of the great being who speaks; "wherever the eternal is taught" is literal.  The mudrā descriptions are terse and several lines are uncertain, especially "whatever becomes separated" in the bathing mudrā and the opening lines of the staff mudrā. "Dull" renders sems ni dur ba, read as dull or sluggish minds. "Your means of accomplishment" (khyed kyi sgrub thabs) is translated as written.  "The Noble Excellent One" renders the vidyā's name literally; it may stand for a Sanskrit name such as Āryabhadrā, which could not be confirmed. "By means of the Moon of noble Tārā" is uncertain: the Tibetan zla bas may mean "by the moon" (perhaps referring to this vidyā, whose mantra invokes the moon), "with a companion", or "within a month". The phrase about the place coming to be "as if in the palm of one's hand" is obscure in the Tibetan and is rendered literally. The speaker at the end of the first section is Avalokiteśvara, whom the text here calls "the Blessed One, the great bodhisattva".  "Tuṭi" renders the Tibetan transcription of an Indian unit of measure (perhaps truṭi), whose exact quantity is unclear. In "stalked plants without fruit, smeared with ghee" the Tibetan reads bar ("between"), evidently a slip for mar ("ghee"), which fits the pattern of the surrounding oblations. The substance rendered "lac resin" (sra rtsi bog) is uncertain. The phrase about making the request "either through someone or directly in his presence" is terse in the Tibetan and its sense is somewhat uncertain.  "Elephant tree" renders glang chen sdong po literally; the plant could not be identified. "King of trees" renders the Tibetan for rājavṛkṣa, and "royal mustard" that for rājasarṣapa, plant names whose exact identity is uncertain. "Ko me" and "nābhāsa" are given as the Tibetan transcribes them; these substances could not be identified. "Eight hundred thousand" follows the Tibetan stong phrag brgyad brgya literally, although eight thousand eight hundred may be meant. In the last rite the Tibetan gnas ("place") after "cow urine" makes little sense; it has been taken as dung, which is uncertain. The phrase "does the covering with it as well" (g.yogs) is obscure.  "Kind and color" reads the Tibetan kha deg as kha dog ("color"), an evident slip. "An effigy of ten palas" reads srad bu ("thread") as srang ("pala"), which fits the pattern of the surrounding rites; this is uncertain. Several substances and woods are given as the Tibetan transcribes them because they could not be identified with confidence: dustira, pushel tsé, ṭāṃpaṇa, dongka, gabina and tsikaseng. "Water of the body" may mean urine. The closing lines of the passage are terse and their sense is somewhat uncertain.  The clause describing Mahāsthāmaprāpta's offering "to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, who had come down among many beings" is obscure in the Tibetan, and its construction is uncertain. In the list of faults the Tibetan sas rdzas appears to contain a stray syllable and has been read as "substances". The sentence beginning "The little recitation of the vidyā" is terse, and its sense is uncertain. "Will through faith itself come within the circle" renders dkyil 'khor bar literally and is uncertain.  "Pāśī" and "kaktukāma" in the neem-seed rite are given as the Tibetan transcribes them; these ingredients could not be identified with confidence. "Camedaka" pulses likewise follow the Tibetan transcription (perhaps chickpea, caṇaka). In two places the text reads "ma pa'i sa bon," taken as "neem seeds" (nim pa) in line with the parallel phrase that follows. The "twelve māṣas" (a measure of weight) given by the son of Vāsuki is ambiguous in the Tibetan, and could be a weight of gold rather than of food. "The essence of dependent origination" refers to the verse of dependent origination enshrined in stupas.  Several readings follow evident copyists' slips: "til" (sesame) in "the sesame that lies in the ocean" is taken as "gter" (treasures), in line with the parallel sentences about gold and jewels; "'gra ba" as "'gro ba" (flowing); "'bur ba" as "'phur ba" (flies); "bad gyi bskal pa" as "bar gyi bskal pa" (intermediate eon). "Realgar bought at a hero's price" renders the Tibetan literally; it may stand for a Sanskrit expression for purchase with "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa), but this is uncertain. "Placing one's hand upon a single sign" is literal; the referent of the "sign" is unclear. "One who desires the king, or the king's garments" is also literal and somewhat obscure. "Living on what the Saṅgha provides" is a tentative rendering of "dge 'dun gyi bstan pa can."  The three kinds of accomplishment over the ghee are rendered by the signs the Tibetan gives ("stirs," "smokes," "blazes"); "stirs" ('gro bzhin pa) may stand for the usual sign of warmth. "Ro ma" here is a corpse, not the subtle-body channel. "Ḍeḍeka," "camedaka" and "the three kinds of rice grain" (tan tu la gsum, taṇḍula) are uncertain identifications. "Iron forged under Puṣya" takes rgyal as the asterism Puṣya, as elsewhere in the text. "Hidden treasure" renders gter sbrag ma, whose precise sense is unclear.  "Lita," "tangzung" (btang bzung) and "tree gold" (shing gser) are unidentified ingredients and are given literally or as transcribed. "Gold" in "oblations of gold" renders gser gyi ngang tshul, whose second element is unclear. "The rank of a kṣatriya" follows rgyal rigs as written, though rgyal srid ("kingship") may be meant. "A cow whose calf is of the same colour" interprets rgyud mtshungs pa'i ba, probably reflecting the Sanskrit sarūpavatsā.  "The royal palace" renders rgyal po'i khab, here a king's residence in a rite for winning royal favor, not the city of Rājagṛha. "Kindling sticks of the brahma tree" renders tshangs pa'i yam shing, likely palāśa. "The other is pacified" reads zhi bar for the evident slip zhing bar. "One should watch for the supreme proclamation" is literal; its sense is unclear. "Being unobstructed" is a tentative reading of ma chod ba.  "The vidyā, together with all that belongs to it" renders rig pa dang bcas pa, whose exact referent is unclear. Several food names in the yakṣa torma (kākamoṭika, sokhavadhi) are transliterated as given and could not be identified with confidence; churba and 'khur ba are rendered as dried cheese and cakes. "Cow dung that has not fallen on the ground" reads sa la ma lhung ba for the written sa lam lhung ba, the standard ritual specification. "Antimony" takes rna ba'i mig sman ("ear eye-ointment") as a calque of Sanskrit srotoñjana. "Anoint the mouth" reads khal as kha la. Rgyal po'i khab here is taken as the royal court (rājakula) rather than the city Rājagṛha, given the context of disputes. Ra sa ris is read as ras ris, painted scroll. The sense of bzhi gas kyang gos so ("even with a quarter, clothing") is uncertain, as is the final phrase tshig bla dags, rendered as "faults of speech."  "Five hundred verses" supplies the unstated object of "five hundred." Several referents are unclear: the thing "revealed" by the khadira peg and guggulu; "water and a knife" (chu gris) for curing poison; karbāpa (perhaps cotton seed, karpāsa); ro ldan ma, given as rasavatī; and sha 'tshong ba, "selling flesh," which may allude to the tantric selling of flesh to spirits. Rtsa ba in the description of the vases is taken as a flaw at the base. Ngang rims is taken as fever. Stong phag is read as stong phrag. The object to be set on molasses and buried at the end is not named in the Tibetan.  "Forgetfulness-causing spirit" renders brjed byed, probably the apasmāra graha associated with seizures. The ailments in the list (ye 'drog, 'bras, phol mig, btsog shu, khyi rngo) are given approximate English equivalents. Several phrases are obscure: the rite of the first mouthful and "outside the proper time"; 'dod pa can thams cad ("all who have desires"); "takes up all distinctions by oneself"; and installing the scroll "on a leaf." The three kinds of accomplishment are warmth, smoke, and blaze, as the text itself explains.  Several items are uncertain: pusīlāka and sauvīra (so so bī rā ma na) are transliterated plant and mineral names; "abode of jasmine flowers" renders sna ma'i me tog gi gnas literally; "bought at a hero's price" (dpa' bo'i rin) is unclear; lus rnam par bcom nas is taken as "having subdued the body"; and "until it becomes a kumbhāṇḍa" (grul bum du gyur pa) is translated as written though its sense here is obscure. Gtum po is taken as outcastes (caṇḍāla), and sdig pa and sdom as scorpions and spiders.  Lhag par rtogs pa, rendered "those of superior understanding," is uncertain. Yungs kar rgyal po is taken as rājasarṣapa, black mustard. Ba bla is given as ox bile and cu gang as bamboo manna; pināka, dongka, and sindhuvāra are tree or flower names whose identification is uncertain. Srang bu is read as srad bu, thread. "Divine oblations" renders lha'i sreg blugs literally.  The first of the three signs is written "from another scent" (dri gzhan pa); the sense is unclear, and "brings all beings under control" supplies an evident missing "control" (dbang) in "sems can thams cad du byed pa". "Hair of a bronze hue" renders skra li, which is uncertain. "To the height of a palm tree" reads tshad for tshang. "Make offerings for one night" reads mtshan mo gcig for mtshan ma gcig. The sentence on being seen by almsgivers in the topknot rite is obscure; it may intend that one becomes invisible to all but the almsgivers. "Pure deodar" renders lha de dri med, tentatively taken as devadāru; the reading is uncertain.  "Coral" reads bye ru for bye rul, which is not otherwise attested; the substance is uncertain. "Recite over scented paste" reads dri la for dril ("bell"), which makes little sense here. "Antimony collyrium" takes rna ba'i mig sman as a rendering of srotāñjana. The solitary liṅga (mtshan ma gcig pa) is the ekaliṅga, a classic site for such rites.  "Ears of grain" takes snyi ma as snye ma. "Cassia" renders dong ka, tentatively. "Milk rice" takes pā mānnā as paramānna. The sentence on the treasure resting "at the depth of a man's height" is obscure; it seems to mean the treasure rises to within reach. "Sound and without blemish" renders the unclear rtsa ba dang nag po med pa.  "Should milk a tawny cow" renders the unclear deb ser skya la bsnun pa; the sense is supported by the parallel instruction below. "Sweeping clean" renders nges par byab pa, uncertain. The sentence about the willow leaves (brkos pas lcang ma'i 'dab ma nye bar mnyam pa) and "large grains" (thug po che) are obscure, and the rendering is tentative.  "Melt" takes gzhu ba as bzhu ba; the corpse passage is terse, and what is melted on its head is not stated. "Tree" renders rkang 'thung ("foot-drinker," Skt. pādapa); abaabīya and sodriya are unidentified plants. The phrase "whoever one's glance falls on" renders gang lung phog pa tentatively, and "together with a single stūpa" (mchod rten gcig dang) is unclear.  "Elephants" renders ཡིད་ཀྱིས་གཉིས་འཐུང, apparently a calque of Sanskrit dvipa ("drinking twice," i.e. the elephant). The tree name བཏྱ་ཊ་ཀ is transliterated as found (vatyaṭaka) and not securely identified. "Burn incense" reads བདག་པ as a slip for བདུག་པ. The ཤཱི before རིམས in the fever rite may stand for śīta, "cold fever." The phrase "made auspicious" (ཤིས་པར་བྱེད) for the finger-snapping mudrā, "the mantras will be roused" (སློང་བར་བྱེད), and "works upon the secret mantras of others" (སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད) are literal renderings of obscure ritual statements. The fasting clause for bringing a man under control is duplicated in the Tibetan and is translated as it stands.  "Bronze" reads ཁྲིའི་ཚོགས་ཅན as a slip for ཁྲོ་ཚོགས་ཅན, which follows it. "Bilva kindling sticks" takes བལ་བ as bilva; the tree is uncertain. "Ocean" reads རྒྱས་ཚོར as a slip for རྒྱ་མཚོར. "Have it painted" takes འདྲིར as a slip for བྲིར. "Sudarśana" renders ལེགས་པར་མཐོང་བ, taken as the name of the discus. Some statements are rendered literally because their sense is obscure: "at dawn the Teacher sets it all aside" (སྟོན་པས་ཐམས་ཅད་འཇོག), "it keeps supplying food" (ཟན་འཕོ་བ), "until it splits open" (ཁ་གས་པ), and the sound "śita" (ཤི་ཏ).  "The conjunction of Puṣya" takes རྒྱལ་པོའི་སྦྱོར་བ as the Puṣya conjunction, since རྒྱལ is this text's name for that constellation. "A goose" reads དད་པ as a slip for ངང་པ, which the rite then names ("until the goose moves"). "Aparājitā flowers" renders གཞན་གྱིས་མི་ཐུབ་པའི་མེ་ཏོག. "Peacock feather" reads རྨ་བྱས་རེག as touching with a peacock. Several slips are read as their evident forms: སྦྱང for སྨྱུང ("fast"), and ཞིབ for ཞི་བ ("pacify"). Two statements are rendered literally because their sense is obscure: "will not pass beyond the wilderness without having thought of it" and "whoever has the garland." The substance taken with milk in the copper vessel is not named in the Tibetan, and nīlāṭaka is not securely identified.  "On a panel" takes འབྲས་བུ་ཅན as a calque of Sanskrit phalaka, "board, panel," confused with phala, "fruit." The final sentence of the passage, listing further qualities of the kindling (green, with dried leaves, or black), is rendered as it stands; it seems to begin a description that continues in the next piece.  This fire-offering section is terse and in places obscure; several lines are rendered literally. Some evident slips are read in their evident forms: མ for མེ ("fire") in "kindle the fire"; བུད་མེད ("woman") for བུད་ཤིང ("fuel"); and རྒྱས་པས for རྒྱལ་བས ("the Victorious One has rejected it"). "The sky's treasure," "those that are firmly set in their place," "a single tongue of flame," and "in the palm of the hand" follow the Tibetan as it stands, and their exact sense is uncertain.  The line "everywhere these are spoken of as censured," following the drum sounds called a certain sign of accomplishment, is translated as it stands; it may refer to the opposite signs, or "censured" may be a slip for "praised," but the Tibetan is kept. "Roaming here in this land" renders 'khor ba in a sense that is not certain here. "Ailments of the legs" renders rkang shu, whose exact meaning is unclear. The clause about the queen ("except for any approach of desire") is understood as excluding sexual union; the phrasing is terse.  Several plant and substance names are uncertain: "piṇyāka wood" follows the Tibetan transcription pi nyā ka; "dongka flowers" keeps the Tibetan name dong ka, which I cannot identify confidently; "lāpana" is kept as transcribed. "Antimony eye-salve" takes rna ba'i mig sman ("ear eye-salve") as a literal rendering of Sanskrit srotoñjana. "Keeping silence" reads mi smra bar for the written mi smya bar ("not going mad"), which does not fit. The fever sentence ("one day, two days ...") is taken as referring to intermittent fevers. The closing sentence about the seal (khug cig, "summon") is terse and its exact procedure uncertain. "A clean place that bears all things" may mean the earth.  "Bhuṣuṇḍala," "saileṭaka," "tārāvartaka" and "girikarṇī" follow the Tibetan transcriptions; the first is probably a kind of club or missile weapon. "Milk" reads o ma for the written po ma. Ba bla is taken as orpiment and gi wang as bezoar (gorocanā). "In the third or the seventh practice" renders a terse phrase whose exact reference is uncertain.  Avalokiteśvara's hymn is extremely obscure in the Tibetan, apparently a mechanical rendering of an ornate Sanskrit stotra whose syntax is not recoverable from the translation; it has been translated line by line as literally as the Tibetan allows, and many lines (especially those naming Śakra, the moon, the pārijāta tree and the ritual bath) are uncertain in their connection and reference. "In verses of one accord" renders tha mi dad pa'i tshigs su bcad pa, literally "undifferentiated verses." "The Bodiless One" (lus med) is taken as Kāma, the god of desire. "All-Seeing" renders the name of the absorption (probably Samantāvalokana).  "Having first disciplined his body by strength" renders a line containing si tha'i lus, whose first word I cannot identify with confidence. "Smooth" takes snun as a variant of a word for an even, soft surface, and "trees" reads ljon shing for ljon shig. "The month of miracles" is taken as the month commemorating the Buddha's miracles at Śrāvastī.  The line about going out "by the measure of the immeasurable Three Jewels" is obscure in the Tibetan and is rendered literally. "Then he should offer water for the face" renders zhal ni srub, which is unclear; srub ("churn") may be a slip. "Jiba flower" is probably the red japā (hibiscus). The list "one, two, three, eighteen, and another sixteen" of those not to be accepted is unclear in its reference (numbers of disciples or ages) and is given as it stands. Ras la nas is read as bsal nas, "having removed"; bre as bri, "draw"; rab dang as rab dad, "deep faith".  Several dream images are obscure: "rohaṇa" and "rahaṇa" are transliterations left as written; "a, dhi and the like" seems to refer to letters or syllables seen in a dream; "the hands of dogs" may stand for dog-cooks (śvapaca), an outcaste group paired with caṇḍālas. The "alāsa made of copper" is an unidentified ritual object, given as transliterated.  Many of the uṣṇīṣa kings and goddesses are named by Tibetan epithets whose Sanskrit forms cannot be identified with confidence; these are rendered by their meaning. Just as the Bodhi tree now standing at Bodh Gayā neither is nor is not the same tree beneath which the Buddha attained awakening, so too this stupa is intended as the next generation of stupa — dependently arising according to the conditions of its environment, and ceaselessly proclaiming the Dharma for the benefit of all sentient beings.

May whoever encounters these words derive great benefit.
